title: Services, Ingress & Cluster Networking
summary: How traffic finds a Pod that keeps changing IPs, from inside the cluster and from the internet.

slides.markdown:
Pods are disposable — a rescheduled Pod gets a **new** IP every time. Anything that hardcodes a Pod IP breaks the moment that Pod restarts. A **Service** solves this by giving a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of Pods, selected by label.

The Service itself never runs anywhere — it's a routing rule maintained by kube-proxy on every node, mapping the stable IP to whichever Pod IPs currently match its selector.

Four Service types, each exposing traffic at a different scope.

| Type | Reachable from | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| ClusterIP (default) | Inside the cluster only | Internal service-to-service calls |
| NodePort | Any node's IP, on a fixed high port | Quick/manual external access, dev |
| LoadBalancer | The internet, via a cloud LB | Public-facing production service |
| ExternalName | Internal DNS alias | Pointing at an external service by name, no proxying |

LoadBalancer builds on NodePort, which builds on ClusterIP — each type is a superset, not a separate mechanism.

slides.subTitle: kube-proxy modes
slides.markdown:
kube-proxy on every node programs the packet-routing rules for Services. **iptables mode** (the long-time default) writes NAT rules that randomly pick a backend Pod per connection — simple, but slower to update as Service/endpoint counts grow. **IPVS mode** uses an in-kernel load balancer built for this job — hash tables, not a linear chain — with more balancing algorithms at scale.

Either way, kube-proxy never touches application traffic directly — it installs rules the kernel executes.

slides.subTitle: DNS-based discovery
slides.markdown:
Inside the cluster, you don't look up a Service's IP manually — **CoreDNS** resolves `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` (or just `<service>` from the same namespace) to its ClusterIP automatically. Every Pod is configured to use CoreDNS via its `/etc/resolv.conf`.

This is why application code just connects to a hostname like `payments-api` and it works regardless of which Pods are currently backing it — DNS resolves to the stable Service IP, and the Service forwards to a live Pod.

slides.subTitle: Ingress vs Service
slides.markdown:
A LoadBalancer Service works, but one per app is expensive with no HTTP-level routing. **Ingress** sits a layer up: one entry point routing by hostname/path to many Services.

![Ingress routes to Services routes to Pods](assets/ingress-vs-service.svg)

Ingress is a *routing rule* — it does nothing alone. An **Ingress controller** (a Pod running NGINX or Envoy) reads those rules and does the actual routing.

assets.alt: Ingress routes to Services routes to Pods

slides.subTitle: Ingress controllers
slides.markdown:
"Ingress controller" sounds like special cluster infrastructure, but it's just a **Pod** — usually a Deployment running NGINX, Envoy, or Traefik, fronted by its own LoadBalancer Service. It watches Ingress objects via the API server and reconfigures its embedded proxy to match, the same watch-and-reconcile pattern as every other controller.

Without an Ingress controller installed and running, Ingress objects are inert YAML — nothing routes anything.

slides.subTitle: NetworkPolicies
slides.markdown:
By default, every Pod can talk to every other Pod in the cluster — flat, fully-open east-west traffic. A **NetworkPolicy** restricts this per-Pod, by label selector: "only Pods labeled `role=frontend` may reach Pods labeled `role=backend`, on port 5432."

NetworkPolicies are **allow-list only** and additive: once a Pod is selected by any policy, everything not explicitly allowed is denied to it — there's no way to write a rule that opens things back up.

slides.subTitle: Public service with TLS at the Ingress
slides.markdown:
Expose a service at `api.example.com` with HTTPS: create a ClusterIP Service in front of the app's Pods, an Ingress object with a host rule for `api.example.com` and a `tls` block referencing a Secret holding the certificate, and rely on the Ingress controller to terminate TLS and forward plain HTTP to the Service internally.

The cert lives once, at the Ingress — individual Pods never handle TLS themselves, and adding a second hostname is one more rule in the same Ingress object, not a new LoadBalancer.

slides.subTitle: NetworkPolicy with no enforcing CNI
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "I wrote a NetworkPolicy, so traffic is now locked down."

**Why it breaks:** NetworkPolicy is just an API object. Enforcing it needs a **CNI plugin that implements it** (Calico, Cilium). Some CNIs (bare-bones flannel, for instance) silently accept the object but never enforce it, leaving traffic open while the YAML implies it's restricted.

**The correct model:** confirm your CNI enforces NetworkPolicy *before* relying on one — an ignored policy is worse than none, since it creates false confidence.
